title: Duke Mu Gives Wine to the Horse Thieves
text:
Duke Mu of Qin ruled in the 7th century BC in what is now western China. According to the Lushi Chunqiu, compiled in the 3rd century BC, one day some of his fine horses broke loose and wandered off. Local country people at the foot of Mount Qi caught them and ate them, about three hundred men in all.

The duke's officials arrested them and expected them to be executed. Duke Mu said a gentleman should not harm people for the sake of an animal. He added that he had heard eating horse meat without drinking wine was bad for the health, so he gave the men wine to drink and let them go.

Some years later, in 645 BC, Qin went to war with the state of Jin at Han. In the battle Duke Mu was surrounded, his chariot was in danger and he was wounded. Suddenly a band of about three hundred men burst through the Jin ranks and fought fiercely to rescue him. They were the men who had eaten his horses. Qin won the battle and captured the ruler of Jin. Sima Qian tells the same story in his Records of the Grand Historian.
lesson: Generosity toward small offenders costs little and is often remembered. Those you treat kindly when you have the power to punish may stand by you when you need them most.
source: Lushi Chunqiu, book 8; Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), Basic Annals of Qin
caveat: The story is a traditional anecdote whose details, like the number of men, may be embellished.
